div.head: THIRD LAP-AND FINAL?
div.p: THE THIRD LAP-AND FINAL?

Yesterday was the second anniversary of the fateful day on which we declared war upon Germany and risked our national existence rather than remain the craven witneSses of the violation of a small and peaceful 'commu- nity we had solemnly undertaken to protect. An unknown and dark future lay before us, but we faced it in preference to the easy but dishonouraba course that we might have pur- sued. We have not regretted, and never shall regret, the choice we made. The experiences of the war, many of which have been startling and ~unthinkable, have in fact taught us once More that virtue is its own reward. Had it been conceivable that the people of these islands could have, even for a moment, fcir- gotten their traditional love of freedom and their history as the champions of the oppressed and the enemies of the tyrant, we should have contributed to our own undoing. We now know the base nature and the fright- ful ambition of the Central Powers. They tried to lull us into a feeling of safety and dis- interestedness, but is there a rational being in the whole world who does not now see that had we stood aside until France and Russia had been defeated, , we should have been tackled in our single-handed condition and reduted to the position that the Germans long

div.head: THE
div.p: THE

to see us occupy? They professed friendship, it is true, but we now know how' to value German friendship. The only way to keep Germans in their place is the way of the bayonet, and we are now about the work of applying that method with effect.

The Kaiser has been celebrating the passage, of time by addressing his "comrades" in the Army and the workshops of Germany; and the contrast between his present-day bombast and his bombast in the early days of the war shows unconsciously that he knows that the whirlwind which he let loose is promising now to sweep him away. The contemptible little English Army that was to be walked over, for instance, finds no place in his present fatherly address. But hei talks of his heroic men in field grey resisting, in "unshaken fortitude, the terrible onslaughts of the enemy." It is, true he claims an unbroken chain of successes; but he goes back pathetically to the fact that they are fighting victoriously " against gigantic superiority." The confidence that Germany is invincible has never left him. But Germany knows she is " fighting for her existence." He is, how- ever, prepared for the third year, whether we wage it by force of arms or "cold, calculat- ing malice." The malice evidently refers to the hold we have upon the gentleman's throat at sea, and not to the calculating malice that sent the Lueitania, with its battalion of women and babies to the bottom of the sea, or the doing to death of a sea captain for daring to save his ship from the Lusitania's• fate. We shall appreciate the Kaiser's bona-fides at the full when we remember that it is at sea where Germans have fought so successfully against gigantic superiority. He puts it an- other way when he says that on "that glorious day" his young fleet inflicted "a heavy blow" on the British Armada. But—again but— "the strength and will of the enemy are not yet broken."

No, not yet. We have strugglecl through two long weary years, and so far from being broken, the end of them finds the Allies in- finitely stronger than when they started. We are just about to begin. All the nations that' joined the fray against this monster that late Nineteenth and early Twentieth Century civilisation raised are more closely knit to- gether than over. They are now moving in unison for the first time, and have suddenly taken the initiative from the foe. We may have a long and a hard journey still before us, but we shall make it, • and the end is certain; and the Kaiser, in his heart of hearts, knows this is so, if he dare not say it. Our men in the trenches and on our warships, and their womenfolk at home, and our munition workers at home have decreed the abolition not of Germany, but most assuredly of German militarism. ,

div.head: GOSSIP.
div.p: GOSSIP.

' Gossip—not "Examiner " gossip I am pleased to say—has again "cut up" our local Ten t- torials. If the Territorials are " cut up" it is at the fact that their native town should possess so mail), imbeciles as to be able to start this distressing rumour so often.

The Ei-a miner " has, already explained, in order to lay this rumour startea a few months ago. that the Territorials are on other than fighting work. A letter from the Colonel re- ceived this week, and dated so recently as last Saturday, speaks of a trek, and shows his men to be still capable of troubling their minds about heat, water, cigarettes and flies!

Those who have been exempted on condition that they join the Volunteer Training Corps have been notified to attend their first parade on Thursday. About 150 notices have been sent out. Eighty have already reported with- out being notified.

It was an inspiring sight to see the& gaudily- decorated quadrupeds moving, sidewise across the Swing Br;dge lest they mtght accidentally knock over a tramcar, and endeavouring 'at the same time to keep their finery untarnished. The foals were also in holiday attire, and evidently thought the decorations extremely long as they lifted their feet much higher than on ordinary week-days. Vanity is vanity.

Now that all available men have joined or must join the Army there is no need for foot- ball clubs, as an incentive to recruiting, to cease playing; and Wilderspool will witness a resuscitation of the game—on a friendly non- competitive, amateur basis—next month.
Men engaged on munitions, or are otherwise available, are invited to play for Warrington to uphold her traditions till the, regular boys come back.

The Northern Union is about to celebrate its coming of age. How? Not by receiving pre- sents or having jollifications or doing its officials well, but by devoting over gsoo of its balance to buying a motor ambulance for use on active service. They have invested £3,000 in War Loan, and last year gave £250 to the Prince of Wales' Fund.

A large proportion of the playing members of the clubs in the Union have fought or will fight for their country in due course. After what our athletes and athletic organisations have done for the country. the early cries of the " antis " look particularly crude.

I , hope that the . Warrington Club, as a recompense for their decided act of , patriotism by closing down altogether last sea Son rather than appear to stand in the way of recruiting, will be favoured by a good team -and bumper " gates " during the coming season.
I was glad to notice on Wednesday night, when a convoy of wounded soldiers passed through the town from Arpley Station to Winwick, that the Warrington crowds had found their voices.

Wounded soldiers arriving here have wonder ad why the people lining the streets have been, practically dumb. The crowds felt like cheer- ing but didn't "like." Some one has 'given the needed start, and I hope the shout will gather in volume as the convoys come.
The men are in good spirits and they expect us to be. Besides, they deserve a pat on the back for all they have done.

A motor driver tells me he has been asked more than once by wounded soldiers why the people of Warrington are so sad. He thinks an effort should be made to show these brave lads that we appreciate their great deeds.

But stand back while you shout. Don't get in the way of the ambulances and cars, as a driver trying to save you from being kille4 may have to swerve and run the risk of further damaging already badly damaged men. Such a thing has already happened.
At the Town Council meeting on Tuesday, Councillor Broadhurst was rather keen on life and death matters.

Wrien speaking of the gravediggers' wages he contended that they were so low that they did not encourage the birth-rate. Verily, the grave- diggers must concern themselves both with the dead and the living!

Speaking later he declared that the high price of electricity "has killed my scheme once, and now you are going to kill it again." Killed twice! According to the legend of the cat it, has still to die seven more times yet. Coun- cillor Broadhurst need not despair.

There are many suggestions as to the manner in which we must punish the Kaiser—when we have caught him. Some, like the Mikado, say "Boiling oil," others "Gas," and others "Flaming Liquid." What I say is make him ride on the top of a Manchester-road tramcar for a week.

HOPES OF A HOME RULE 'HELPING ON THE VICTORY SETTLEMENT. Favoured with beautiful weather, about 300 members of the Liberal Women's Sewing Class sat in the charming grounds surrounding Col. Crosfield's residence, Tower House, Bewsey, on Monday afternoon, and. after a few hours' work and a short respite for tea heard interesting speeches delivered by Sir Arthur and Lady Crosfield and Mr. C. R. Parker, following which various games were played, Lady Crosfield giving the prizes. Mrs. Osborne, the hon. secretary, expressed the pleasure they all felt at having the Presi- dent (Lady Crosfield), Sir Arthur Crosfield, and Miss. Elliadi with them again, remarking that it seemed like o/d times once more. (Ap- plause.) Amidst general regret Lady Crosfield an- nounced that Colcinel Crosfield would not be with them as he had been called to a committee meeting of the National Service League, under the chairmanship of Lord Milner, in London, that afternoon. He was very sorry not to be present at that gathering in his grounds. If he had been there they would all have given him a hearty welcome back to War- rington. (Applause.) It was very kind of him to allow them the use of his charming grounds, and they all acknowledged with pleasure his kind hospitality. (Applause.) Although it had been a long time sijace she had met the members of the sewing crass, her Ladyship said she always knew of their doings, for Mrs. Osborne, who was such a splendid leader and organiser, kept her well posted up with news. Mrs. Osborne had told her of the good work they had done during the winter, and how proud she was that they had all worked in such a fine manner. Many of the members had brought gifts and, in particular, she wished to give her hearty acknowledgment and thanks to Mrs. Per- cival and Mrs. Collins;who, through the holding of a series of whist drives, recently contributed £5O to the funds. 'and had to-day brought an additional £l2. (Applause.) Mrs. Percival and Mrs. Collins had, therefore, done splendid and devoted work, in addition , to which their "better halves" or—should she say?—" worse halves" had followed their examples ana covered fifty card tables with green baize. Applause.)
Work For AIL

"From one or two remarks I have•heard fall • this afternoon," continued her Ladyship, " believe some of you think that when I am not in Warrington 1 lead a very lazy and indolent life, invariably sitting on a couch, clad in a tea gown, and reading the latest novel. (Laughter.) Well, that is really not my vocation. (Hear, hear.) I have been busier than ever recently, for the 32 beds in the Voluntary Aid Hospital, of which I have the honour to be the command- ant, have been increased to 43. This has in- volved a great deal of work, but we have the gratitude of the authorities and the patients for what we are doing." (Applause.) There was no reason or justification far anyone to-day to sit with folded or idle hands. Members of the War Workers' Sewing s Class led

busy lives, but she might tell them something which they could pass on to others :1' there were not enough workers for our hospi- tals. Those who wished to give their services voluntarily to. the Red Cross Society or Volun- tary Aid Detachments could do so, and those who could not afford to keep them- selves would be paid •by the Red Cross Society. That society and all our military hbs- pitals were Willing to pay for services rendered. At one time they had to hold certain certificates before being accepted, and they would not take ladies who had had no previous experience. To- day, the only qualification demanded was a pair of strong and willing hands. (Applause.) She ! hoped that those who could come forward to help would do so. -

They were all proud to be wearing their War Badges, next remarked her Ladyship. They must not relax their efforts in the slightest, but go on steadily, without any slacking Off. "I want us to keep up that character of per- sistency," she 'added. (Applause.) "We have a splendid opportunity of proving that we really deserve the vote, but I will not speak about that, for politics are barred. What we want to do is to go on working and working at new garments and woollen goods, and literally smother our soldiers in them, so that they will not feel the cold if there has to be another winter campaign. It rejoices my heart that you are working so hard in the good cause." (Ap- plause.)
For Humanity's Sake.

Sir Arthur Crosfield amused the audience by saying he regretted he had mit been able to he present to hear his wife address them, because he , was invariably accustomed to get some "tips " from her for any speech he was to deliver. s He added that it gave him great pleasure to meet the stalwart workers of the Liberal party of Warrington, who had done such admirable work for so long during these terrible times. Might he congratulate them not only upon the MI6 work they had done for the lads at the Front, but on the persistcint way in which they had done it? He thought it .wias a characteriitic which they showed in common . with those at the Front. It was not only the daring, dash and magnifi- cent grit of the Lancastrian—referred to again and again by our Commanders-in-Chief—but their persistency, which the Liberal women of Warrington shared with them, that was spelling the death-knell of the Prussian gospel of brute, force and insolent ascendancy over Europe, which had brought such disaster upon the nations of this continent. For the ladies to have carried on that work week after week and month after month, under the admirable inspiration of their secretary, Mrs. Osborne, and under the able leadership of herself and the ladies associated with her,—this had meant a sacrifice and one felt very proud to realise how readily the women of Lancashire had made that sacrifice for the great cause we all had at heart. They had only got to read the news- papers to see what that sacrifice meant, and he did not think that on a pleasant afternoon like that he would spend too much time in trying to bring before their minds the grim realities of the awful business. What he would rather emphasise was the magnificent work being aehieved here and now in Europe. The sacrifice was appalling, but, black as the cloud was, he thought it was well for them now and again to turn their eyes to that familiar old silver lining, for they all had the satisfaction of knowing that what their lads were now doing on the battlefields of France was part of perhaps the greatest piece of work for humanity it had ever been given to mortal man to accomplish. (Applause.) That afternoon he was not going to try to develop all that would follow the war, but he would say that the destruction and the overthrow of the reckless, brutal, insolent, and unscrupulous doctrine of force was the greatest achievement possible to mortal man. (Ap- plause.) Alluding to the ,way in which the whole Empire was united to a man in this •struggle, Sir Arthur also referred to the colossal mis- calculations and fatuous assumptions which had led the Kaiser and his Prussian colleagues to persuade themselves that the outbreak of hostilities would mean the disruption and the dismemberment of the Empire. Well, they did not need a European catastrophe to prove Colonial loyalty. They all knew that before the war the loyalty of the Colonies was splendid. But now in this supreme crisis of the Empire's history it seemed impossible to express in any adequate ,terms the depth of feeling, deter- mination and devotion which was, cementing the foundations and strengthening the bonds of the Empire 4n a way that would last through untold centuries. (Applause.) Ten thousand ,years might roll by and still by the log fires of Canada, and in the recesses of the Australian bush,. the great deeds achieved by the Empire's soldiers in this war would be celebrated, and historians would almost be inclined to rewrite history and date as from the year 1 the whole sequence of events that was going to follow the Armageddon being fought out to-day. div.head: Sick Of Extremists.
div.p: Sick Of Extremists.
BY."THE EXAMINER" MAN.

Alderman Bennett. makes a point of seeing, first-hand, as much as possible of all passing events. Does a Colonial Premier pass through Warrington ' Station? Alderman Bennett, by some mysterious agency, knows the exact moment, and though he stand alone on the platform, he is present to bid the passing celebrity "Goodbye." Does a steeplejack build his ladder to the dizzy height from which the great brass cock keeps watch over the irinds and the town at the top of the Parish Church steetde? The Alderman takes the chance to look upon his native town from a point at which an eagle would be more at home than an alderman. Even kings cannot be crowned or monarchs interred in the absence of Alderman Bennett. It was natural, therefore, that an "Examiner" man should ask him whether he had been across to Dublin to see that city in its rebel- lion-blighted condition. Of course, the Alder- man had been. Would lie recount his experiences? Certainly he would. In the Alderman's philosophy, the next important thing to acquiring knowledge is to impart it to others. "What was the object of your journey?" I asked. _ .

"I have always been keenly interested in the Irish question," said Alderman Bennett. "I have visited the country many times and was anxious to see how Dublin looked after the rebellion, and to ascertain by personal inquiry the prospects of the compromise in reference to Home Rule."

Alderman Bennett proceeded to tell me of the scenes of ruin and desolation that met him on entering the city at the moment Mr. A squith's interesting statement as to the basis of. the Irish settlement was published in the newspapers. Most of the main -facts are well known, but, told with the Alderman's freshness of treatment and picturesqueness of language, the story; which he will doubtless publish in full some day, was remarkably illuminating.
WHERE THE TWELVE APOSTLES STAYED.

"Across the O'Connell Bridge—an even wider bridge than ours," he said—" I reached O'Con- nell-street, or Sackville-street, to use its ancient and familiar name. The sight that greeted me was simply shocking. When last I had been there it was still one of the most beautiful streets in the world. To-day, the wer portion was a heap of ruins. There was not a single building standing on the right side of it until I reached the street beyond the Nelson Pillar, and the ruins extended down the river quays almost as far as the Amiens- street Station. The buildings on the left bore many marks of the bombardment, and of the Metropole Hotel, where I stayed with the Twelve Apostles' in January, 1914, not a vestige now remained, save bricks and mortar and accumulated debris. "A man I met described to me a futile attempt ,to blow up the noble Nelson monu- ment, but it towered up in the middle of the street as majestically as when I saw it first some two-and-thirty years before, and, for the sake of ` auld lang syne,' I climbed its 166 stone steps again and gazed, with mingled sad- ness and amazement, on the far-stretched scene of havoc spread below, ringed in by an the spires and towers and roofs of the great city, with the grey sea to the east and the blue mountains stretching hazily away towards the south and west."

div.head: ABOLISH CASTLE RULE.
div.p: ABOLISH CASTLE RULE.

At the Castle the Alderman saw the spot where the policeman who happened to be on. duty when the rebellion started was shot dead in cold blood. "A friendly member of the Force conducted me inside," he said, "and showed me the rooms in which poor Mr. .Birrell had managed to make such a mess of things, the Vice-regal headquarters, the chapel and all the other outward and visible signs of what has long been known as 'Castle Rule.' The sooner we abolish it the better. .

"In a detaxled tour in a jaunting car, in the course of which I visited the Glasnevin Cemetery, the man who guided me devoted practically all his time to pointing out the. wonuments .of Irish martyrs for the last hundred years or so. Some of them I, too, could honour, `rebels' tho Ugh they were, but I rather 'drew the line at O'Donovan Ressa, and the incident was I strangely typical of nearly everything I had heard that day." 1 "How do you think the political situation has been affected or modified by the war and the rebellion?" I asked this question, knowing the uncompromising attitude the Alderman had held for years on the question of Home Rule, and having intimate knowledge of his readi- ness, in spite of any and every consideration, to examine and review problems in the light of new, facts. "I love Ireland and the Irish passionately," he said, "but they are a curious people and hard to satisfy. I have not hitherto admired John,Redmond much, but since the war began I think that he has tried to play the game. No ,living man has laboured harder for what he believes to be the interests of his country, but I did not hear a single kind word said of him', and the prevailing opinion seemed to be that if he were to contest his seat he would be defeated, whilst everywhere, except among the Unionists, none of whom appeared to be satisfied with the ,new scheme, I fancied I de- tected latent evidence of admiration for the men who had laid some of Dublin's proudest buildings in the dust."

div.head: SURELY!
div.p: SURELY!

"And what is your opinion, as a Unionist, of the proposed settlement?" I asked. "It is unthinkable," replied Alderman Ben- nett, "that the loyal men of the North should be forced into subjection now; and, thanks to Mr. Redmond, Mr. Devlin, and, Sir Edward Carson, each of whom has acted with good sense and magnanimity, the basis of a settle- ment had been at last secured. Surely, amid the horrors and pre-occupations of this fright- ful war, we ought to welcome it, especially as it is meant to be only temporary and is subject to revision when the war is over as part of a great Imperial settlement which should satisfy us all. I am sick of extremists and the contretemps this week in the House of Com- mons is really heartbreaking. I am equally disgusted with the anti-Redmondites and the disgruntled Unionists. If nobody will give way and there is never to be any wive-and-take or any spirit of mutual accommodation, the task is hopeless. It was that which wrecked the conference immediately before the war. If everybody will be reasonable we may settle things to-morrow; at any rate, until the war is over; and then, in consultation with the Colonies, build up, upon a federal basis, a really United Ireland as part of a really United E m vire "

div.head: CHANGED BELFAST.
div.p: A CHANGED BELFAST.

Alderman Bennett continued his pilgrimage to Belfast on the eve of the Twelfth, but every- thing was strangely quiet compared with the excitement of previous times. Ancient feuds had been forgotten in the common losses of the war: The only flag he saw upon the way was one at half-mast. In the loyal capital itself," he said, "instead of the usual flaunting banners picturing King William riding proudly through the Boyne, I saw only an occasional Union Jack, the drums were almost mute, and in, stead of Boyne water' the song they sang was Keep the home fires burning till the boys come back.'"

As the six counties were to be left outside the Home Rule Parliament, Unionists, while holding that a Parliament would not do any good to Ireland, were content, as their leaders had agreed upon a compromise, to acquiesce and turn their thoughts to the graver struggle raging across the sea. . The Nationalist attitude was frankly unfavourable; Unionists appeared to be almost indifferent; but everybody seemed to think the question was more or less settled. "And, to-day, through somebody's folly, all the efforts of the last Tow weeks seem likely to be flung away. To me," the Alderman con- eluded, "the thing is pitiful." - •

Williams, who served in France for some time, but was iilvalided home with frost-bite and ii now at Wrexham. He 'wrote as follows: "Just a few lines to let you know that I heard the very sad news of Bill, your son and my best pal, killed in action. I was going with a firing party to a funeral in Mold and saw a chap out of my platoon home on leave, and he told me I the sad news. Will you, and all the family accept my deepest sympathy and that of all the boys in the barracks from our battalion in your sad bereavement. It is a very big blow to you, I know, but I hope from the bottom of my heart that God will give you strength to bear it. There is one thing you can know—he died a hero and he was well liked and respected by all the boys who knew him. He had done his bit well."

Corporal Monks had been in the Army almost eighteen months, and at the Front since December last. ,He 'recently celebrated his twenty-first birthday. After leaving Heathside School he was apprenticed as a wood turner to Messrs. R. A. Naylor, Ltd., but had latterly been in the employ of Messrs. ThoS. Whittle and Son, Ltd., Rose and Crown-street.

div.head: PRIVATE THOMAS HEWITT.
div.p: PRIVATE THOMAS HEWITT.
Took Leading Part In Greatest
Victory Of The War.

Private Thomas Hewitt, of, the machine gun section of the King's Liverpool Regiment, eldest son of Mr. and Mrs. Thomas Hewitt, Maples, Latchford, was killed in action on the first day of the great advance, July Ist.

The official intimation was conveyed in a letter written by an officer to Private Hewitt's parents in the following terms : "My officer having been killed in action I have been promoted to his position, and so to me falls the sad pleasure of writing to express on behalf of the Machine Gun Section our appreciation of your son's work for us and for his country. The whole section join in an ex- pression of our deepest sympathy at your irreparable loss. His death was caused by a shell, and was quite instantaneous. You will live to be proud that he took a leading part in the greatest victory in the war, and one which will appreciably shorten it. There is still work

to be done. Ality we all face the future as un- flinchingly as your son, a true soldier, who met a soldier's encl.—Yours in deepest sympathy, E. J. SUM, 2nd Lieutenant." Private Hewitt, an "old boy" of People's College, was 25 years of age, joined the forces in August, 1914, and had been at the Front for nine months. lip to the outbreak of the war he carried on a building and contracting busi- ness, in succession to his father. He was a member Of the Warrington Cycling Club, and St. Paul's Football and Cricket Clubs, and his bright and sunny disposition had iron Mr

1914, having been previously employed by the St. Helens Cable and Rubber Co., Ltd. He was educated at the Latchford R.C. School. His brother, Private William Hastry, whose home address is 96, Algernon-street; is serving with the same regiment, and it was he who sent the news, on . Tuesday. The body was brought to Warrington on Tleursday and will be buried with military honours to-day (Saturday). ,Captain J. O'Connor, in command of Private Hastry's company, writing to Mrs. Hastry, under date August 2nd, says :—" As officer commanding the company, I wish to express to yourself and family the most sincere sympathy of officers, N.C.O.'s and men of my company on the sad loss you have sustained by the death of your husband, Private Hastry, who died suddenly whilst in the execution of his duty. He was a good soldier and did his work cheer- fully and without complaint; and it came as a great shock to me and his comrades to hear of his untimely decease. It may he some conso- lation to you to know that he has given his life for his country just as surely as if he had fallen in action. May God in His mercy en- able you to bear your great loss with fortitude and may his soul rest in peace !"
PRIVATE J. HASTRY. Died from Shock.

div.head: PRIVATE J. HURST.
div.p: PRIVATE J. HURST.
Son Of An Old Soldier Who
Served In India.
Missing since August 7th, 1915, Pte. JosePh Hurst, of the Lancashire Fusiliers, and son of Mrs. Hurst, 22, Bank-street, is now officially reported to have met his death on or about that date.

Private Hurst, who was 20 years of age, was the son of an old soldier, his father, who has been dead some years, having served in India for nine years. Educated at St. Mary's School, Private Hurst was formerly employed at the Grappenhall works of the Richmond Gas Stove and Meter Co., Ltd. He enlisted soon after the outbreak of war.

Private Widd, who is 28 years of age, was formerly employed at the wagon works of the L. and N.-W. Railway Co. at Earlestown. He enlisted in November, 1915, and had been at the Front only seven weeks. The other soldier brothers are Sergeant Thomas Widd; of the South Lancs. Regiment, who was awarded the Military Medal a short time ago for distin- guished conduct in the field, and Private Walter Widd, a dispatch rider in the King's Royal Rifles. He was wounded in July last year. A fourth brother was formerly in the Army, but has been discharged.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 5, 1916.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 5, 1916.
SERGEANT R. E. BURTT.
IV3-cliffe School Teacher Suffering • From Shell Shock.

A Warrington .school teacher has been wounded, in the person of Scrgeant Richard Ernest Burtt; of the R.A.M.C., whose home address is Hawthorne-grove, Stockton Heath. He is now in No. 3Western General Hospital, Cardiff, and writing from there to Mr. S. W. Jeffery, headniaster of the Aryellff School, he sayg:— _ .
"As you will see by the address I am in 'Blighty.' I have been wounded, but only Slightly. It happened on the 14th. We had
SERGEANT R. E. BURTT. Wounded.

an advanced dressing station there and were surrounded with batteries, for which ' Fritz ' was busily searching. We were right on the old line of trenches and used some of them as sleeping places, store and cook-house. I had been on since 1 a.m., having a fine view of the bombardment. About 4 a.m. we began* to be very busy until about 10 a.m., when things began to slacken a trifle and we slipped off by twos and threes for a bit of 'grub.' I had just gone round to the cook-house and was sitting with three others when a high explosive shell landed on the side of the trench. The other three were killed outright. I was thrown violently against the side of the trench, knocked unconscious, and partially buried. When I came to and was got out I was very much shaken, and sore and bruised generally, with a big abrasion on my right arm. I was sent down as 'shell shock,' and after a few days at Rouen landed here on the 20th. I am feeling quite well now, except for slight stiffness and soreness in the muscles of my neck, back and arm. " My arm is almost healed, so that I expect in a few days to be sent either home Or to a convalescent camp." Sergeant Burtt, who has reached his thirty- fi •

Arst year, was formerly a teacher at the Wycliffe School, Bewsey-street. He enlisted in February of last year and went to France the first week in August. He was educated at a Birmingham College, and had been at Wycliffe School about eleven years. He has two brothers in the Army, one of whom has been an inmate of a Torquay Hospital for a con- siderablb time. The other, a Second-Lieutenant, is serving in France. They are the sons of the Rev. R. A. Rurtt, of Highgate, London.

div.head: CORPORAL E. LUNT.
div.p: CORPORAL E. LUNT.
Recovered From Chapelle Wounds And Again Wounded.

Corporal' Elijah Lunt; of .the Rifle Brigade, son of Mrs. E. Lunt, 42, Howley-lane, has been wounded a second time. The first occasion was at Neuve Chapelle in May last year, when he sustained injuries to the right thigh and left arm. He has now been wounded during the great advance and is in a Croydon hospital, with two feet damaged by grenades and a gun- shot wound in his arm. He was in the first rush on July Ist, but came through that ordeal safely.. After After ten days' rest he went forward in support and was wounded on Sunday, July 23rd. He reports his general health to be good and his wounds to be progressing satisfactorily. He has been promoted Corporal since he was previously wounded, when he was a rifleman. Twenty-eight years of age, Corporal Lunt is a good. bowler. He is a member of the Bull's Head Bowling Club. As a boy, he attended the Hamilton-street School, and on leaving there
PRIVATE J. 11. ATHERTON.
Receives Six Wounds Whilst Collecting Wounded.

Private .James Henry Atherton, of the South Lancashire Regiment, was wounded on the 19th 'July, and has been brought to a Birmingham hospital suffering from wounds in both arms and thighs, and below the ankle—six wounds in all. He has been visited by his mother, who found him very cheerful. Writing on July 21st from. France to Mrs. Atherton,. at 28, Forster-street,. Sergeant Wood- ward said :—" Your son has-, unfortunately, been wounded, and asked me to write and let ' you now. He was quite comfortable when taken to, hospital,. and very cheerful. No doubt he will write himself in the course of a few days. Might I add tliat itwas a pleasure to work with your son, for he was a cheerful lad, and did his work as a soldier should. He has done his bit with credit to himself and you, and 1 sincerely hope he will recover from his wounds and soon be back again in his home." A comrade; Private G. Y. Houghton,- wrote : "He was bringing in wounded when he was hit. He was, always plucky, and did not care for anybody."' Private Atherton, who is 20 years of age, and an only son, has been in the Army for eight months, and at the Front seven weeks. He was formerly employed at the Longford Wire Works, and was educated at St. Benedict's R.C. School.

he entered the service of the Warrington Tanning Company, in whose employ he con- tinued till September Ist, 1914, when he en- listed in Kitchener's Army. He departed for the Front on the 27th of January last year.

He has a younger brother, Clifton Lunt, in the Warrington Territorials, w,ho has been at the Front for eighteen months. His nephew, Edward Percy Challinor, is in the Royal Fusiliers (Public School Battalion). Tlie late Mr. Edward Lunt, father of the wounded( soldier, was a well-known Warring- ton contractor.

div.head: PRIVATE 'J. BARTON.
div.p: PRIVATE 'J. BARTON.

Reservist Three Times Wounded In ,The Finger. Private J. Barton, of the Border Regiment has been wounded in the finger for 'the third time. Writing to his parents, Mr. and Mrs. J. Barton, 73, Pierpoint-street, he says:—" They are trying hard for it, but they can't knock it off.. We are giving them something, for their 'money now, I can tell you. They are frightened out of their shoes with our artillery bombard- ing them, and then the lads at them with their , bayonets put the 'top hat' on them. . . . All they can say when you get near them is "Mer/y, comrade,' after the way they have treated our' men. They were told they had only Kitchener's fools to face when they came over to us and they thought they had a walk-over. But when they came they found the thin khaki line wait- ing for them with machine guns and rifles, so they got a gentle reminder for their cheek, and they will not forget it for a long time." Although only 21 years of age, Private Barton, who was called up as a _special reservist im- mediately upon the outbreak of war, has seen some very hard fighting, including that at Mons, where he was first wounded. Ile was educated at the National School, and before, being called 4 up was employed in the netting department 4t 17.ylandb Bros. Ltd.

div.head: PRIVATE F. BOOTH.
div.p: PRIVATE F. BOOTH.
Wounded In The Thigh After Nine Months' Service.

Private Frank Booth, of the Manchester Regiment, whose home address is at 45, Orford- avenue, was wounded in the left thigh on the morning of the 23rd ultimo, and is now in hospital at Bristol. He was visited by his wife and mother on Saturday, who found him pro- gressing as well as can be expected. Private Booth, who is 22 years of age, enlisted in September, 1914, and has been at the Front nine months. He was formerly employed at Peake's Warehouse, Manchester, and was
I. RIFLEMAN H. COOK.
Brought To Lord Derby Hospital With
Shell Wound In Foot.

IThe eldest of tht three soldier-sons ,of *Mr. and Mrs. Thomas Cook, 5, Kent-street, viz., Rifleman Harry Cook, of the Rifle Brigade, has been wounded and was brought to the Lord Derby Hospital on Wednesday night. Inform- ing Mrs. Cook of her son's misfortune, Sergt. P„ Bond wrote, on July 24th : 'Your sort 1'164 the misfortune to get wounded this afternoon, July 24th, but I am glad to say IL is not a dangerous\wound. A piece of shell struck him In the foot, and I am hoping that he will have the good Tuck to get to the old country. He was a good soldier, a \ good worker, and always got on well with the rest of his comrades. I hope that you will hear from him soon and that he is progressing well."

-Rifleman Cook, who is 35 years of age, was formerly employed' as- a wiredrawer by Messrs. Rylands Bros., .T.to.. and was educated at St. James' School,,Lat:hford. Re enlisted a week after the outbreak of was, along with three other-brothers, and had been at the Front over twelve months. The three brothers who ere., listed with him are: Oswald Cook, who is serving at Salonika with the R.F.A.; Wallace Cook, also of the R.F.A., but since discharged; and Stanley Cook, of the East Lancashire Regi- ment, also discharged. Another brother, James Cook, is in training with the South Lancashire Regiment, having been enlisted 'since March. The remaining son is only 16 years of age. The father, Mr. Thomas Cook, is an employe of Messrs. Fletcher, Russell and Co., Ltd.

Charnock, of the South Lancashire Regiment, that he has lost a finger of his left hand while in action. He is now in hospital at Manches- ter and hopes soon to be transferred to War- rington. Private Charnock, who only celebrated his eighteenth birthday a fortnight ago, has been in the Army about sixteen months and at the Front seven months. He was employed at the Leffigford Wire Works before enlisting, and was edueated at St. Ann's School. His father, Mr. William Charnock, is in the South of England with the National Reserve.

div.head: MISSING.
div.p: MISSING.
PRIVATE. C. TALBOT. Nothing Heard Of Him Since June 18th.

Nothing having been heard of Private Chas. Talbot, of the Lancashire Fusiliers since June 18th, considerable anxiety is being felt as to his fate. He last wrote to his parents, Mr. and Mrs. W. H. Talbot, 21, Eldon-street, upder date, June 'lBth, when he said: "I have just been ordered to stand-by to move up the line any minute." Since then Private T. Timperley has written to a friend from the Front saying that Private Talbot was killed. Another Warrington soldier wrote home saying that lie had been talking to some men of the Lancashire Fusiliers, who also said Private Talbot was killed. - -

Private Talbot, who was in his 22nd year, joined the Army in September, 1914, and after twelve months' training was drafted to the Front, where he was slightly wounded in the foot by shrapnel in May. Educated at the National School, he was formerly employe(' by Messrs. Rylands Bros., Ltd., was a good billiard player, and interested in swimming. His brother, William, is a driver in the R.F.A. at the Front.

div.p: GUNNER S. KAY.
Wounded In The Shoulder By A Shell.

Gunner Stanley Kay, of the signalling section of the R.F.A., son of Mr. Wm. Kay, 19, Willis- street, has been wounded in the shoulder by a- shell. div.head: BLUES AND GREYS..
div.p: THE BLUES AND GREYS..
Wounded Soldiers Revel In Sports At Winwick.

The blue and grey figures of scores of con- valescing soldiers raced about a plateau to the West of the Lord Derby Hospital at Winwick on Wednesday afternoon, in various competi- tions included, in the annual sports. As many of the hundreds of wounded soldiers who were fi to be out in the open—and the number was vast, tor the weather was glorious—Were pro- vided with comfortable accommodation to watch the fun. Some of them appeared in fancy dress, one " Tommy " sporting Oriental clothing, which he may have brought from India or bought from Linga Singh. Another was dressed as a perfect lady out for a stroll in the Park. Her partner was a comrade im- pressively attired in a morning suit and a silk hat worthy of Tattersall's at Ascot. Tilting the bucket, the obstacle race, and the tug-of-war (international) were the most in- teresting and amusing items. The tug-of-war was tremendously exciting, but the Scots beat the English, Welsh and Irish. As they pre- pared for the pull and began to fix their heels in the ground an enthusiastic shouted,. "Dig yourselves in!" There was no need: they easily won The Big Pull. Among the spectators were Surgeon-General Hathaway and Mrs. Hathaway, the latter dis- Iributing the prizes, which were provided from the comforts' fund. By CRITIC.
The great offensive has commenced and the lads out there have proved their mettle.
Lymm, although but a small place, has been well represented, and in the near future some thrilling tales will be told of the part played by Lymm lads during the great Hun retreat.
We have had our fair share of casualties, and some of our gallant lads have gone under. I should like to take this opportunity of ten- dering my deepest sympathy to their loved ones.
May we ever think of these heroes in the true light, for they have sacrificed their all tor you and me!
And may their loved ones be consoled in the knowledge that they have died the noblest of deaths, fighting for Right and Liberty against Might and Brutality!
The charming weather that we are now ex- periencing daily adds to the charm of the village and brings its fair share of visitors.
I notice that we are atoured, as of old, by the well-known "Monday afternoon women."
I am very pleased to notice that someone has placed yet another seat at the corner of the New Lever-road for the benefit of our wounded heroes.

div.p: " Tommy's " heartiest thanks is theirs.

And only right, too.
I am very sorry to hear that a well-known public thoroughfare is getting a very bad name through women congregating together ana gossiping.
A few thoughtful moments by those con- cerned can easily remedy this.
I hear that 13 Belgian refugees left Ought- rington Hall for France. during last week-end.
The thing that impressed me most during my visit to Oughtrington Hall was the splendid way in which .everything was managed.
Every man and woman has his or her own particular work to do, and although there is quite a large crowd there, no one is allowed to be idle.
The children are mastering the English language in splendid style, and are able to con- verse quite fluently.
I hear that a cricket match had been arranged for our wounded soldiers during the past week, but owing to there being too many leg cases it was cried off.
Since the appearance of the aeroplane last week several people in the village are suffering with strained ,neeks.

His stated time of service having expired he is entitled to a month's furlough before re- joining his unit.

div.head: COUNCIL'S PROTEST.
div.p: COUNCIL'S PROTEST.

Germans In England. Councillor C. E. Cowper, at Monday's meeting of • Lymm Urban Conned, moved that. h ving in view the welfare of our allies antl the lads at the Front, all Germans, whether naturalised or not, should be interned. Councillor Gotobed seconded. They would not be alone- in passing such a resolution. It had been done in various parts of the country. He was quite sure if they, as Englishmen, were, living in Germany, they would not be allowed' _ _
_ the freedom that Germans had ix•this country. (Hear, hear.) The Chairman (Conn. F. Lockyer) asked if it was meant to refer to their district. Councillor Gotobed: No. All through the country. _
The resolution was passed, and a copy was directed to be sent to the Prime Minister.

div.head: "SHAKE HANDS."
div.p: "SHAKE HANDS."
Reconciliation Of Councillors Gotobed And Parker.

Whether or not the salubrious weather which has recently made Lymm more charming than ever, produced a mellifluous effect upon the " inclined-to-be-stormy " side of Councillor G. H. Parker at the monthly meeting of Lymm Urban Council on Monday, or that the naturally brusque and good-humoured feelings of that gentleman suddenly went out on a wave of.sym- pathy to his fellow member, Councillor R. H. Gotobed, there was quite a touching scene before they left the Board room. As a journalist of the old style would retord, when the business portion of the meeting had terminated, Councillor Parker, rising from his seat, said: Gentlemen, at our last monthly meeting I made a certain charge against Mr. Gotobed. " No doubt I said more in the heat of the moment than I had intended. I have seen Mr. Gotobed since, and he has given me to understand that what he said to me was meant to be taken in a jocular spirit. Anything I have said to Mr. Gotobed I withdraw. (Applause.) A Councillor (admiringly) : That's a manly spirit.
-Councillor Gotobed (in subdued tones) : I accept that withdrawal, Mr. Chairman, in the spirit in which it is made. (Renewed applause.)
Another Councillor: Shake hands!
They did so warmly, then left the Connc Chamber and walked down the road together.

div.head: A% %It ALLOWANCES.
div.p: A% %It ALLOWANCES.
Payments To Council Employes In Jeopardy.

The question of continuing war allowances to soldier employes was again raised at Monday's meeting of the Lynam Urban Council, when Mr. J. Hardy Holt (vice-chairman) said that at their last meeting it had been decided to refer the matter to tne General Purposes Com- mittee. There was no report, and he under- stood that it had not been dealt with at all. Had the question been suspended? The Chairman, (Mr. F. Lockyer) said he did not know. He thought it would have been .before them that night. Mr. Groves said it should be definitely under- stood that it was to be brought forward at once. 1 The Clerk (Mr. MuHard) suggested that a ' note should be made to bring it forward at a meeting of the General Purposes Committee to be held the fallowing Monday. Mr. bit: Do I understand that the payment is stopped? The Clerk : No, it is going on yet. Mr. Holt submitted that when the matter was questioned no payments should have been made. Any payments so made were out of order. The Clerk: The original resolutiotio has not been rescinded. Until it has been rescinded the payments go on. Mr. Holt took exception to this method of doing Council business. -It was understood that the question would be discussed at their next General Purposes Committee. Now the thing was allowed to go on and suspicion was aroused that payments were still being made. The business of the Council should have serious and urgent attention in the interests of the rate- payers, and if it had not, he would resign. Mr. Gotobed said that he was responsible for havitig this matter referred to the General Pur- poses Committee. It was now decided that the matter should be discussed at the meeting next Monday. The Chairman said the Clerk was ill at the time, and he went to see him. Mr. Mullard told him that until the original motion was rescinded they could do nothing. The Glerk : I was not present at the !fleeting.

Mr: bit: I think it is very unsatisfactory that the thing should be allowed to drag on. The Clerk read Mr. Holt's motion, handed in at the last meeting: "That all allowances to Council employes now serving with H.M. Forces be discontinued, and that each case be decided on its merits and dealt with accordingly." To that resolution an amendment was proposed and carried referring the matter to the General Pur- poses Committee. He (the Clerk) now advised that it would first be necessary to call a special meeting to rescind the original resolution. It was agreed to call a meeting for next Monday evening.

div.head: FALL FROM A TRAIN.
div.p: FALL FROM A TRAIN.
Belgian Refugee Child's Miraculous
Escape.

Master Jacque Culen, a Belgian refugee, late of Oughtrington Hall, who is a. present stay- ing at Didsbury, had a miraculous escape from sudden death whilst paying a visit to his old home on Saturday last. It appears that ,the boy, who is only six years old, was travelling to Heatley Station on the 9.45 a.m. train, accom- panied by four elderly people and four chil- dren. When the elderly people were engaged removing their luggage from the rack he inter- fered with the carriage door handle and was thrown from the train, which was travelling at the rate of 40 miles an hour, with terrific force and fell in the 6 foot. Some plate- layers, who were engaged on repairs, at once conveyed him to Dunham Massey Station, where on examination by Dr. Leonard Thorpe, who was summoned from Lymm, he was found to be suffering from nothing worse than severe bruises and shock. After a short time he was able to proceed to Oughtrington Hall by ear. .He recovered sufficiently to be removed to hi 3 hOrno at Didsbury.

div.head: AFTER THE PUSH.
div.p: AFTER THE PUSH.
Private Percy Clare Comes Home For
A Month.

With the dust of Flanders still upon him, Private Percy Clare, of the Cheshires, arrived home late on Tuesday night. Calling at his residehce at Booth's Hill, our representative found the gallant soldier peacefully reclining and apparently enjoying a well-earned rest. Private Clare's period of service has expired and he has been granted a month's furlough, prier to -rejoining his regiment. He had come direct from Franca and had been in the great push. The gallant soldier is very modest, and though our representative is one of his parti- cular friends, he absolutely declined to talk about the great deeds they have done. How- ever, he assured him that the Lymm lads had "come out all right" and were in the best of health. His particular duties lie with the transport, and their work is to see that their comrades• in the trenches are supplied with every .necessity, and, in the event of a move, to transport their heavy luggage. Private Percy Clare, who is well-known to "Examiner "readers as a gifted correspondent, was mobilised for service at the commencement of war and was drafted out to France in February, 1915, where he has had some very exciting experiences. He was, prior to the war, employed as a gardener by Mr. Houghton, West Legh. He is a prominent footballer and vtas a playing member of the local club. For several seasons he was a member of the Lymm Lads' Club.

div.head: IN HONOUR OF THE BRAVE.
div.p: IN HONOUR OF THE BRAVE.
Laurel Wreath Placed On The Historic
Cross.

A touching scene was witnessed on Thursday, evening, when. Mrs. T. J. Ridgway, Wilders- more, placed a beautiful laurel wreath on the historic Lymra. Cross, in memory of the gallant lads who are fighting and beating the treacher- ous Hun. The ceremony was performed in the early part of the evening, and through the whole affair being kept a secret it was only witnessed by a few people, including several Councillors and children. As the wreath, which was made entirely of laurel leaves, knotted by a large bow of red, white and blue ribbon, was being placed into position, the company present realised the thoughtfulness of the scheme and scarcely a dry eye was to be seen. A pleasing, yet striking feature, was noticed when the young boys present fell into line, and, standing at attention, saluted the wreath in respectful manner.

div.head: "We Will Remember."

div.p: MR. H. S. SAVILLE'S APPEAL FOR HIS SON.

The case relating to Mr. H. S. Saville, which the Tribunal some time ago refused to hear, was dealt with by the local Tribunal at the last meeting! - Mr. - Saville, a well-known local business man, appealed for the total .exemption of his son on the grounds that he was the only man of military age left in his employment. He

has an extensive business, which- covers' a smithy, 1.4 e sale of agricultural implements, and motor haulage work. Tile son appealed for was manager of the agriculture and motor department. He had advertised for _labour and also offered to sell his business, but had met with no results. In connection with the motor haulage trade he was engaged in transporting material from local shops to Sheffield. He also did a lot pf emergency work in connection with the 10-cal doctors, taking serious cases to

the infirmaries. In support Of his appeal let- ters were read from the Lancashire Tool Co., British Plier Co., Sheffield Scissor and Razor Co., Dr. Burrows, and the District Nurse. div.head: LIEUTENANT W. W. UTLEY.
div.p: LIEUTENANT W. W. UTLEY.
Home On Furlough After Suffering
From Trench Fever.

Lieutenant W. W. 'Utley, of the R.A.M.C., has this week arrived home on a month's fur- lough from the Front. He informed our re- presentative that he had been serving with the Field Ambulance during the great push, and while carrying out these duties he had contracted trench fever, which had forced him to be admitted into, hospital. He, however, was well on the road to recovery, and at the end of his month's furlough he hoped to return to the Front.

Lieutenant Utley is a very popular local offi- cer and is widely interested in sport, being a playing member of the local Cricket Club. Up to joining the Army he was president of the Lymm Angling Association. He also is a popular member of the Conservative Club. In civil life he holds an important position under the Salford Corporation, and is also a qualified medical man. He is married and 'resides ,with his wife at Brookside, Brook-road. lie re- ceived his commission about 13 months ago and went out to France early in April.

"Unjust as Untrue."—Mr. W. Stewart Royston, Sunnyside, Paddington, writing to a London weekly respecting a statement in an article to the effect that "the Church has done nothing," says the statement is unjust as it is untrue. "In this parish," he continues, "our young and popular Vicar volunteered his ser- vices as Chaplain to the Forces in August, 1914 ,before the word ' shirker ' was heard of. In- stead of living on here in the calm and quiet of a country vicarage with his young wife and four little ones, he is to-day cheerfully endur- ing the hardships of the ' dug-out ' with men who were members of his flock in 1914. The chief diocesan here, although approaching his seventieth year, insisted on relieving a son whose spiritual was invaluable in the diocese at the commencement of the war. And not only that. Three other sons have joined the Army, while a sister is to-day ministering to the sick and wounded in France. Such cases could be multiplied many times." div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.
‘VOUNDED SOLDIERS ON THE
GREEN.
Fifty From War Hospital Welcomed By Tannery Workers.

One of the most striking results of the Great War in this country is the splendid bond of sympathy which has been created between the worker and the soldier. Supremely gratifying is the compassionate interest shown by workers towards our wounded men, and on Saturday afternoon an excellent treat was given by employes of the Penketh Tanning Company tce a number of soldiers from the Lord Derby War Hospital. A War Relief Fund, contributed to by the men and supplemented by grants from the firm, has been in existence for some time for the purpose of assisting various beneficent projects, and the committee, of which Mr. George J. Dale is secretary, thought it would be a nice idea to invite fifty wounded soldiers from Winwick as their guests. The proposal had the hearty approval of the company through Mr. J. G. Withinshaw, managing director, and the fine bowling green and lawn tennis courts, provided by the firm for their employee, were placed at the disposal of the military visitors. _ _ .

A bowling match was arranged, for which prizes had been kindly given by Mr. E. A. Murphy and Mr. W. B. Moston. The soldiers were fetched from the hospital to Penketh by the company's big motor lorries, which were comfortably seated, and on their arrival at the grounds were most hospitably received by the committee. The day was beautifully fine and the tennis and bowling matches were entered upon with great zest. The workmen mixed freely amongst their guests, and cigarettes, toffees and fruit were lavishly distributed. At five o'clock the company adjourned to the vil- lage schoolhouse, where an excellent knife and fork tea was provided. The lady members of the staff and other friends presided at the aifferent tables. After tea the games were resumed and about nine o'clock the visitors said "au revoir" ,to their hospitable hosts, 'laving spent' a very happy time and received much benefit from their outing.

An official communication has this week been received by Mrs. George Drinkwater, Sandy- lane, to the effect that her husband, Private George Drinkwater, 'of the South Lancashire Regiment, has been wounded. It, however, appears to have been a mistake, for his parents at Rush Green have since received several communications from him, in which he appears to be quite well. An extract of one of the letters is, El s follows: _ -

"Do not worry about Thomas (a brother) being Wounded, for he will be quite all right and possibly have the good fortune to get to England. We have just been in a big battle, but, thank God, we have come out all right. We have now removed to another place and it is a lot quieter." , Private George Drinkwater, Who is a married man with four children, enlisted at the out- break of war, and was drafted out to France about eleven months .ago. CORPORAL VALENTINE PLINSTON.
Popular Athlete Dies On Active
Service.

Mr. Edward Plinston; of Orchard-street, Stockton Heath, has been informed that his brother, 'Corporal Valentine Plinston, of: the Royal Field Artillery, who formerly resided with him; has succumbed to disease in Meso- potamia. The news was quite unexpected, as two letters written in a cheery style were re- ceived last week from Corporal Plinston, bear- ing date 26th June. He stated in one of these that he was suffering_from a mosquito bite, but was now convalescent, and was bathing in the sea every day. He also said that he expected to "have a pop" at the enemy in the course of a few days, and added the rather prophetic words that the country was "no white man's land."

Corporal Plinston, was one of 15 employes of Messrs. Pearson and Knowles Coal 'and Iron Co., Ltd. who joined the Army in a bunch in September, 1914. He was only 24 years of age, having been born in 1892, and was educated in
_ Arpley-street School. He was a member of the congregation of St. Thomas' Church, Stockton Heath.
This fine young soldier was a most popular athlete in Warrington, having been wicket- keeper in Cairo-street cricket team, and also an

div.head: REMOVAL OF REFUSE.
div.p: REMOVAL OF REFUSE.
Lack Of Acid Causes Warrington To Withdraw Help.

The important question of removing ashes and nightsoil is engaging the serious attention of Stockton Heath Parochial Committee. At their meeting on Tuesday evening (Mr. G. Pilling in the chair), Mr. Hough (clerk) read a letter from Warrington Town Council stating that owing to the Government having stopped all supplies of sulphuric acid, they could not under- take to treat an night refuse from Stockton Heath district. They had made urgent repre- sentations to the Minister of Munitions, but without succem. They would therefore be obliged to terminate the existing arrangement with Stockton Heath by August 19th, and would be glad if the committee would try to cease deliveries before that date. They were sorry that they were not in a position to help further, but the committee would see the ditS- culty in which they were. The Chairman in reply to Mr. Pearson, said the first intimation they got on this matter was on the let July.

Mr. Charles Dukes said they had no idea that the shortage of sulphuric acid would be likely to lead to this. The Chairman: No, we had no idea. Mr. Dukes suggested that they themselves should write to the Minister of Munitionsofl the subject. Mr. Pearson said they might write to War- rington and suggest that they should make a joint appeal to the Minister of, Munitions. Mr. Dukes thought as the quantity of acid required to treat the sewage was not very much, they might get permission for some to get through. Mr. Westbrook said something would have to be done. The Parish were almost solely dependent on Warrington taking the excreta.

On the motion of Air. Pearson- the Clerk was requested to write a letter of appreciation to the Corporation, and embodying the suggestion already referred to. The Committee then consulted in private as tc proposed methods of dealing with the difficultv, and Messrs. Pearson, J. Hallows, Westbrook and the Clerk were appointed to make inquiries in a certain quarter. Amongst the accounts passed for payment wag one for the supply of four dozen galvanised ash-bins at us. each, £26 Bs.

div.p: Wounded, Taken Prisoner, And Rescued.

Writing to his parents. Mr. and Mrs. Frederick Smith, The Poplars, Stockton Heath, on August 2nd, Private Cyril F. Smith, King's Liverpool Regiment, states that he arrived safely the previous night at Bristol General Hospital, and that he is going on all Tight. He continues, "I was wounded in the right thigh

and right hand about 5 a.m. Sunday morning, in attacking the German trenches at I was lying in a shell hole about an hour, when I was picked up by one of our men, iv ho was taking back two of our wounded meit, and three prisoners. Owing •to the mist they unfortunately led us to a German trench, where for about half an hour we were made prisoners until a party of our fellows came to our rescue. About thirty a the Germans immediately gave in and came over to our side with us. A lucky let off for us. I am afraid our platoon. lost rather heavily, our officer being killea . • • - I had twenty-four hours sat No. 8 Stationary Hospital at Winereuse, near Boulogne. I crossed over to Dover and came to Bristol, where we had a good reception, being provided with tea, cake and cigarettes. , I have had a fine time 4nce being here, having the best of food and attention." Private Smith, who is an only son, joined the " Pals " Battalion shortly after the beginning of the war, and has served long and arduously in France. He was educated at Wallasey Gram- mar School, and was employed in the office' of his Grammar School, and was in the office of his godfather, Mr. John H. Welch, ,chartered accountant, 8, Harrington-street, Liverpool. Private Smith was formerly, a member of Stockton Heath Hockey Club, from whence he transferred into the Northern Hockey Club, having its headquarters at Crosby. He was also very fond of golfing, and belonged to the Mersey Golf Club.

If Mrs. Lamar Stanleigh was in a quandary, Esther was equally nonplussed. The documents so rudely brought to light in the gipsy camp told her the Stanleigh secret: .

"Dr. Henry Lee will testify that, the little daughter of Colonel Stanleigh disappeared the night the Colonel died. I took this child because Stan- leigh took my baby boy. She has been brought up as my child and known as Esther Harding.—EUGAß HARDING."

At last the girl knew the truth. She was Esther Stanleigh, of Stanleigh Hall, and Arthur was not her brother, but Arthur Harding, son of Hagar. She was in her rightful place at Stanleigh Hall, for she was Esther Stanleigh. But she resolved, through the love she bore for him she had known as Arthur Stanleigh, that she would take the secret to the grave. She would spare Arthur the shame she knew his proud spirit would feel: What to her was place and position in Fairfax among a proud people who, as far as their womenfolk were con- cerned, had ostracised and ignored her? Yet when we are young we have .our hopes and dreams. Esther's hope and dTeam was the return of Arthur, the sharing of the ilecret with him, and his love. Then all would be well. So it was that Esther was not wholly surprised when Blair Stan- leigh's mother called at Stanleigh Hall and prof- fered her friendship and assistance. There were no confidences exchanged between them. Esther suspected that Blair's mother vaguely knew, but in bet loneliness, and having no friend save the humble though devoted Quabba, Esther was glad • to accept the advances made by a woman whbm she had previously ‘distrusted, though neither spoke of the tie. •_ . .

Mrs. Stanleigh suggested that Hagar be taken to Richmond for treatment for her mental affliction. She also insisted that Esther should go to Rich- mond and be introduced into the best circles there by Mr's. Burton Randolph. Consequently she wrote to Mrs. Randolph:

"My Dear Cousin,—l do not believe Blair mar- ried that adventuress, Vivian Marston. There are strong reasons why we must get Blair to return. You must also -receive and entertain 'Esther Hard- ing. For urgent family reasons -I desire him to marry her.—Very cordially. Euss firkru.nun."

Mrs. Randolph did not understand the "move," as she inelegantly termed it, but acquiesced in the desire of her and a few Anys later, Esther and Hagar were escorted to Richmond bx the widow. Quabba had been left behind at Staineigh Hall, but he was suspicious of Blair's mother; she was probably an old foe with a new face of friendship. "You're right, Clarence," he said to his monkey. "We'll go to Richmond and watch over our little mistress. I don't trust those people."

Smarting under their defeat at the hands o, Blair, Tom Blake and Abe Bloom called to see Mrs. Stanleigh when they heard she was in Richmond. The detective arranged the meeting, and Bloom was particularly anxious to meet the mother of the young man who had bested him, especially after receiving a telegram from Vivian: "Blair and I have parted. Train robbers lifted the diamond. Wire 500 dollars. I'm broke." The loss of the diamond nearly broke Vivian's heart. Now that it had gone she had no further need of Blair and left him callously. "You fool. I only married you for the diamond. If you attempt to stop me I will betray you to the police." Bloom was not in the best of moods wheit he met Mrs. Stanleigh. "You make good this bad cheque of your son's," he said, "and me and Blake won't say nothing or cause your son any trouble. But there's one thing else. I've got to have this big stone what you aristocrats of Fairfax County call The Diamond from the Sky. My brother advanced money on it, and even if he hadn't that's my price for keeping , my mouth shut," he added, "and I'll see that Blake here says nothing, neither." "But the diamond has disappeared. We don't know where it is," said Mrs. Stanleigh, coldly, though in her heart she raged at the presumption of the grasping, vulgar gambler. "It'll turn up. them big stones always do. It's one of the finest in the world, but that's my price!" retorted Abe Bloom. "If it ever turns up no one can dispute your title to it. There ain't, another one like it in the world. But when you Staaleighs get it, it comes to me! That's under- stood and agreed, eh, Blake?" There was a strange., imperturbable gleam in the keen eyes of the detective, who had maintained his usual tacitnntity 1 during the :strange conference, but he nodded his' head and answered, quietly: "Yes, that's understood and agreed." "Your son can return to Richmond and won't be arrested for murdering that old doctor, but if the diamond is recovered, I am to get it, under- stand?" and with that parting shot, Abe left the widctw with her own thought.. - Thinking always of the diamond, Blair wondered what had happened to the train robbers. He had not learned that, chased by the sheriff and his men, the robber with the diamond had been shot, the jewel falling front his hand as he pitched from the saddle. Another of the men had been killed. together with his horse. On the horn of the saddle hung a bag of looted treasure. Riding that way a month later, "John Powell," in search of missing sheep belonging to the farmer employing him, found by the skeleton of a horse which had made a buzzard's feast a bag of treasure which made him a rich man, The diamond was lying near, gleaming is the sun. but "John Powell," blinded with delight, did not see it, and there it remained—for whom? 'Within a very few minutes the trainmen regretted • their haste. Their disregard of Arthur Stanleigh's Warning cost the passengers dear. It was a most eoccessful hold-up, /and the bandits made a rich haul, including 'The.Diamondutrona the Sky. Vivian had contributed to *her own downfall. Boasting of 1110 value of the great sparkling gem, she had ,4aunted her good fortune in the face of fellow- q.avellers. When a bandit demanded the money and jewels of one of the women passengers she eDitefully said. " You haven't troubled to search that woman." pointing to Vivian. Both Blair and Vivian heard the remark, and ,as Vivian clutched at her breast. Blair rose from Iris seat. "Sit down!" came the demand enforoed bY a levelled gun. "You hand over your jewels." " I have none," lied Vivian. '" Don't believe her, she has a wonderful diamond," said the jealous Dassenger, and Vivian had perforce to hand it Over. All for naught had Vivian married Blair, and a very mad couple left the train at Los Angeles. Once more the New Yorker's schemes nad gone awry. The destruction of the -gipsy camp had been more fatal to the tramps than to the gipsies. Hagar and Esther , were dazed but unhurt, - and with quabba returned to Stanleigh Hall, whilst Luke Lovell 'congratulated himself upon a marvellous eseaPe. Quabba did not disguise his satisfaction When he saw what he believed to be the crushed body of Luke beneath .an upturned caravan, but the gipsy was not dead. He was badly bruised, and eventually limped away and hid while he Planned to make money from the Stanleigh secret. Luke intended emulating Matt Harding and be- come a rich man. Only documents were in what he regarded as a treasure chest, but they were treasures of themselves. One of the old papers revealed that Hagar's husband had dealt with the gentry of Fairfax in his own flesh and blood. Here was a fortune to be gained. Which way should he go to work? There was no one at Stan- leigh Hall to pay him for keeping or for telling the Stanleigh secret, but Luke Lovell knew enough of the Stanleighs and their feuds to realise his best market would be with Blair Stanleigh's mother. If Arthur Stanleigh, so-called, was Hagar's son, a gipsy chang,ling, then Blair Stanleigh was the real heir to the Stanleigh earldom and the diamond. But at the portals • of the home of Blair Stan- leigh's mother the proud, cold widow would hold no traffic with the sinister gipsy who clamoured at her threshold with a secret to sell. She ordered him to be gone and professed no interest in the ware he hinted he hafl for sale. Ellen Stanleigh was, in her austere way, as un- scrupulous in her family ambition as even the grim, cold Judge Lamar Stanleigh had been. But she would have nothing to do with such as Luke Lovell. She realised only too well that once such a, creature had her in his power, even as a con- fidant, his -dominion would be, is is always the dominion of the ignorant, brutal and untenable. So Blair's mother dismissed the chagrined gipsy in cold disdain. . .

" If you have any secret to sell, take it to some other market," said the Widow Stanleigh with cold hauteur. "Unless you leave my premises this Instant I shall have you arrested and committed for attempted blackmail! Shout your secret from the housetops, if you please. I am not concerned." That was sheer bluff, though Luke Lovell was Tot to know it. His brain could not fathom the depths of intrigue in which the Stanleigh's had for generations dealt. div.head: Colonel Crosfield At Works' Bowling Final.
div.p: Colonel Crosfield At Works' Bowling Final.
LADY CROSFIELD PRESENTS
CUP AND MEDALS.

It was fitting/ when Colonel G. R. Crosfield renewed his acquaintance with a Warrington audience—at the final of the Works' Association Bowling Competition at the Horse and Jockey Inn on Saturday afternoon—that he should be accompanied by Sir Arthur and Lady Crosfield, at whose home at Highgate he stayed fUr several weeks soon after being wounded. The welcome the party received when their motor car drew up was a demonstrative one. Play was in progress at the time, but the players held back their woods to cheer along with the large number of members of the association present. It was a cordial reception amid appropriately picturesque surroundings, Flags and bunting, excited bY the breeze, flapped vigorously, and the party wits con- ducted to a specially decorated awning, from which they viewed the sport. It was as a Royal Pavilion, and one ventures that the writer was not the only one to note how the royal emblem across the frontispiece, synchronised happily with the initials of the Colonel him-
' Also having a place of honour under the awning were Miss Elliadi (sister of La•ly Crosfield), Mrs. E. ,Osborne, and Mr. and Mrs. W. Peter Rylands.

After the 'game in which Crosfield's (Cheshire) went down to P. and K., the " Finlayson " cup and gold medals were presented by Lady Cros- field, the hon. secretary, Mr. W. Patrick, first announcing letters of apology for absence from the Mayor (Alderman Peter Peacock) and Lady Greenall, both speaking in high terms of the services Colonel Crosfield has rendered on the battlefield.

. Mr: Patrick added that the members of the Works' BowlingsAssociation were proud of their President. They sympathised with the Colonel in his misfortune and in having to come away from the Front when "The Big Push" was beginning. They rejoiced that he had had a very successful recovery, for they had all been greatly anxious about him. Regarding the Association, Mr. ,Patrick hinted that the time had come when they should have greens of their own to play on, as, owing to their large nUm- bers, they had reached the limit for' that green. If the members of the association did their bit toward that enterprise he had no doubt that the geneleinen of the town would :assist them. It was simply a start that they wanted. (Hear, hear.) In conclusion, the Secretary spoke of the war charities helped by competitions played under their mils.

COLONEL CROSFIELD CONDEMNS PREMATURE PEACE. Aided by his crutches, the Colonel then came forward on to the green, and, speaking in that straight and sincere way of his, assured them that it was a- very real pleasure to see them all again and to have watched the excellent bowling which they always saw on such occasions. He congratulated the Chairman (Mr. John Willett), the Secretary, and the committee, on the way they had kept going during the war, and on the patriotic manner in which they had supported local war funds. It would have been an awful pity if they had not been able to continue the useful work the Association was doing, because, after all, when men had laboured strenuously in their employment they required recreation. (Applause.)_ - While he was with the Territorials the Association sent out half a dozen footballs. "I can tell you that our fellows appreciated them very much indeed," remarked the speaker, "for we had many a good game with them." Out there they thought a great deal of Warring- ton, and Often the old town was a -source of in- spiration to s them. On one occasion they had a particularly tough job on hand, and he re- marked, "Men, remember what Warrington expects of you." They said, "Yes, we will re- member Warrington!" And they 'dug like Trojans, and got the job finished in good time. (Cheers.)' Continuing, the Colonel said he did not know whether they expected him to tell them when the war would be over, or what they were going to do with the Kaiser and the Crown Prince when they got thera—(laughter)--but he would say that sometime this year Germany would offer terms in some roundabout way, and he wanted Britishers to be on their guard. There was a stop-the-war section in this country who were waiting for that moment, and had got leaflets to flood the country as soon as that moment came. We must, however, be firm, and he was sure the audience agreed that we must not stop the war until we had got our own terms. (Cheers.) We must fight on until we got what , the Prime Minister had laid down, until we got it definitely settled that all conquered territery was to be restored, that France was to have Abace-Lorraine, and that indemnities should be paid to the countries which, had suffered. "It is up to you to knock on the head at once the making of a peace with 'terms less than those," the Colonel' declared, amid cheers. "War, of course, is a very terrible thing, but it has its redeeming features. It does shake us all up. It gets us out of the rut, and, you know, it is an awful mistake to be ' rutty.' " In conclusion, the speaker advocated the setting up of "a real, representative Imperial Parliament." "Get an Imperial Parliament representative of the whole Empire, because in the future we have to work together as an Empire. We have got to get away from the 3akish pump." (Laughter and cheers.)

div.p: LADY CROSFI ELD'S " FAVOURITE " LOSES.

Lady Crosfield having presented the cup and medals, Dr. Armstrong, on behalf of the two bowling teams run by Messrs. Joseph Crosfield and Sons, Ltd., handed her Ladyship a beau- tiful' bouquet of , roses. and carnations. A vote of thanks having been accorded her for her services, she said she knew that women were accused of being very strong partisans, and she ought to tell them that throughout the game she had a slight weakness for Crosfield's team. (Laughter.) Nevertheless, she was delighted that the best team won the day. (Applause.) She hoped, however, that next ,year Crosfield's would have another try, and, perhaps, come out winners. (Laughter and hear, hear.) Some- one had accused Crosfield's team of being ner- vous because of the Colonel, 'Sir Arthur and herself being present—(laughter)—but she did not think anyone going under that name could be nervous; at any rate, they had proved that they did not suffer from " nerves " at the Front. (Laughter and cheers.) In conclusion, her Ladyship thanked the association for the gift of £lO made a few weeks ago, adding that it arrived at a time when the Liberal Women's Sewing Class was in slight difficulties and it helped to tide .them over. In replying to a vote of thanks to the vice- presidents, Mr. W. P. Rylands remarked that, if it were possible, everyone connected with works should subscribe to the funds of the association, for it was doing a great deal for

the maintenance of the heith and happiness of working men. Mr. Rylands, on behalf of the Unionist Women's Sewing Class, also thanked the association for the ,ClO sent them.
