Fourth Handicap. The fourth handicap in connection with the Green Dragon Bowling Club, Heatley, took place on the green adjoining the hotel on Saturday afternoon. The weather was everything that could be desired, and the turf was in excellent condition. Upwards of SO members took part in the preliminary rounds, and some excellent sport was witnessed. The great- est surprise of the day was the defeat of Mr. L. Wilson, one of the favourites, by Mr. H. Bell, who won a splendid game by nine points. In the semi- final rounds, which were witnessed by a large crowd, Mr. A. E. Davies beat Mr. Fred Ingham, and Mr. J. Hinde beat Mr. H. Robinson, both games being pretty evenly contested. Owing to the failing light the stewards decided that the final tie should be contested on Monday evening. When the finalists, Messrs. A. E. Davies and J. Hinde. met on the Monday evening, the enclosure was crowded with spectators, and after an exciting and most interesting game Mr. A. E. Davies came out the victor by a score of 25 points against 17 points. Mr. Bolton, the club's president, was the donor of the prizes, the first being worth I', 2 10s.

A Considerable number of business cases were dealt ;with by the Tribunal at the Town Hall on Tuesday. Mr. Swallow, Solicitor, appeared for Mrs. Griffiths, licensee of the Cheshire Cheese, Latchford, who asked for exemption for her son, aged 38, a married man with two children, who has managed the business since her husband's death eight years ago. Mrs. Griffiths is 72 years of age and in poor health. Mr. Swallow pointed out that it was requisite owing to the situation of the house that it should be managed by a man. If applicant's. son was taken, she would only have to employ another man, and it would require someone having experience in the trade. The, Chairman (Dr. Joseph, deputy-mayor) said there-were other similar cases to this one, in which licensees' managers were concerned, Which were adjourned until the Tribunal could consider the whole lot together, .taking into Iconsideration, of course, the special points in individual cases. The present application would also be adjourned. Mr. Swallow: To any particular date?
The Chairman: You will have notice of the decision.
Confectioner's Vanman.

Mr. C. H. Unsworth, solicitor, represented Messrs. Bennett and Son, bakers and confed- tioners, who applied for exemption for a van- man, aged 39.. There-was also an application by the man on domestic grounds, his wife being in delicate health. Applicant has five children. • In reply to the Tribunal, applicant said that he delivered goods in Warrington and Latch- ford. The firm had horse vans and motor vans, and some girls were employed. The employers' appeal was refused, and the decision on the man's domestic application was postponed pending more definite medical evi- dence as to the condition of the applicant's wife. Two Brothers Killed.

A moulder, married; with three children, applied for exemption. He mentioned that he was now earning about .22 a week. He had had two brothers killed in the war, and another is at present with the colours. He Stated that he had been employed .with a certain munitions firm, and had been stopped. He was the only married man stopped—a single man, 27, being kept in his place. • The Chairman (to the Military Representa- tive): Do you hear that, Capt. Mathams? Capt. Mathams : I do. The Chairman asked applicant how much he had been earning with the munitions firm, and he replied from .P.. 3 to £4'a week. The Chairman: 'You ought to have a bank book with that.
The Applicant : I had one bank book for doctor's notes after finishing moulding. (Laugh- ter.)
The appeal was refused. Metal Firm's Application.

Mr. Arthur Browne, solicitor, appeared 'for Messrs. G. Howard, a firm doing an extensive business in the metal trade, who sought exemp- tion for four of their employes and one of the partners. Mr. Browne detailed the large con- tracts which the firm had in hand at present, and the duties of the men referred to, who are all skilled wotkers. They were doing business with no fewer than 34 controlled firms in differ- ent parts of the country. The partner had to visit these places and superintend operations at the Folly-lane siding, where the premises were 34 acres in extent. The firm had at present two thousand tons of metal in scrap to be delivered, and the men were working on Saturdays and Sundays—seventy hours a week. All the firms they were supplying with metal were munition manufacturers. Since the war eight men had gone to the Colours: There are eleven perma- nent men, all over military age except one, who had been six months in the Army and dis- charged sick. There were seven casual labourers.
'The Tribunal grunted conditional exemption in. the cases of all the men except one, in which the application was refused. The partner's case was adjourned. Demands of the Grocery Trade.

The extensive firm of Messrs. • Henry Milling and Co., grocers and provision Merchants, War- rington, applied for exemption on behalf of three of their men. Mr. T. S. Steel explained that some employes had been called up, and that two other men were out sick. The application was in respect of men who were absolutely in- dispensable. Conditional exemption was granted in respect of two employes, while three months was allowed in the remaining case. _

An application by one of the directors of the firm, who has been passed for garrison duty, was again adjourned. Member of a firm making coffins and supply- ing funerals was given two months', final. He is an attested man, aged 38. When asked by Dr. Joseph if he had passed the dcetor he renlied. "Yes, sir, you passed me." Mr. T. S. Steel appeared for a travelling showman (houp-las, cocoanut shies, &c.), aged 34, married. lie goes from town to town for weekly fairs, and rents frontages at so much per foot from local authorities. He said that in some cases these pitches were rented before- hand, being secured three months and even twelve months in advance.—Two months' exemption. Mr. Steel also represented a furniture dealer and mattress and bedding manufacturer, who asked for exemption for his principal employe, aged. 38 years. They manufactured something like 3,000 beds and mattresses during the year, and amongst other institutions, supplied mat- tresses to the WhitecroSs Hospital. This man also acted as clerk.—Two months' exemption.

div.head: "HAPPY TO GO."
div.p: "HAPPY TO GO."
Pianist Whose Wife Has Got A
Situation.

Another sitting was held at the Town Hall on Thursday morning. "My wife has now got a position in town, aud in a few weeks I shall be most happy to go into the Army. I want to go," remarked a pianist, aged 39 vars. "But I should like t) see how she gets loon for a bit." The Tribunal gave him a month. Pawnbroker's Useful War Service.

Mr. Thomas Domville, a pawnbroker with three shops, said that at present he had four men, one of whom was over military age, and he appealed for the others, these being managers. Mr. Domville mentioned that since the war he had done about a thousand miles in his motor car on military work and 4,000 miles on Red Cross work. In his shops he was hard pressed, for, though his business was quieter in the pledge department, it was far busier than formerly in the sales department. Two of the men put in domestic appeals. These the .Tribunal dismissed, granting cOnditional exemption kin' bu4iness grounds to one and giving a month's temporary exemption to the two others.

Mr. Domville said it would mean that he would have to close one of the shops. The Chairman (Councillor Joseph) advised him to try women, but Mr. Domville said he didn't like the idea of a lady managing a pawn- shop. The Chairman: It is astoni.shing what you can do if you are put to it. Mr. Domville: I do not think I have been selfish. I have done my best.

The Chairman: We 'cannot reverse our de- cision. We are very sorry. Later, the Chairman announced that fresh evidence had been brought forwari and, instead of the exemptions being final, they would he allowed to remain open. Run On Mineral Waters.

Mr. Arthur Browne, solicitor, appeared for Messrs. Stothert and Sons, mineral water manu- facturers, who applied for a married man with five. children. He looked after the machinery am' also drove one of the motor lorries during several hours of the day. In consequence of the hot weather they were very busy, and the male employes had to work last Sunday to cope with the business. The firm paid a great deal of money under the new taxes. Before the war began they had eleven males, now they only had four. The man appealed for also put for- ward domestic grounds, these being that his wife was in ill-health as Well as several of his children. • _
Conditional exemption on both grounds.

div.head: FOREIGN, BUT NOT
div.p: FOREIGN, BUT NOT
TURKISH.
Shipping Clerk's Respite.

At the Warrington Rural District Tribunal on Wednesday the shipping clerk of a Man- chester firm engaged in the export cotton trade applied for conditional exemption on domestic grounds as well as on business grounds. His firm wrote stating that applicant was an ac- complished linguist and spoke Spanish and Portuguese. He was invaluable in their busi- ness and could not be replaced. Applicant had been previously granted three months' tem- porary exemption._
Thj Rev. A. M. Mitchell: Is this an English fitm?
Applicant: A naturalised British film. The Chairman (Mr. George Mather) : What country? _ .
Applicant: Syrian. Captain Mathams : It's not Turkish?

Applicant: No. Temporary exemption was granted for two months—this decision to be final. Market Gardener. Mr. Arthur Browne appeared for a market gardener, of Croft, who applied for exemption in the case of his son, 22 years Of age, unmar- ried. It was stated that applicant is unable through illness to attend to his business. Six acres of land are being cultivated as a market garden and are looked after by the son, who also attends to two greenhouses. There are also a horse and pony to take produce to Warring- ton Market, which the young man attends three times a week. Mr. Browne further ex- plained that applicant was in a pitiable con- dition with locomotor ataxy and unable to get up or downstairs. He had not seen the present crop sown in the land. , Temporary exemption was granted until the end of September. Appeal Refused. An employe in a leather factory, whose work consists principally in stamping out boot soles, asked for further exemption; his firm having previously procured a concession for one month. He is 29 years of age, married, with one child, and had been passed for labour service at home or abroad. He stated that he contributed to the support of his father. He has four brothers, all married men, employed on muni- tions. The appeal was disraissed.

div.head: Brewer's Foreman.
div.p: Brewer's Foreman.

Mr. Richard Forshaw, Burtonwood Brewery, requested the Tribunal to grant exemption for the foreman in his bottling department, who is aged 36 and is a married man with six chil- dren. Seven girls were employed in the bottling department, and Mr. Forshaw explained that quite a number of his employes had been taken.
Conditional exemption was agreed to. Other Cases.
The farm bailiff of the Padgate Cottage 'Tomes, a married man, aged 37, and for whom his employers appealed, was given three months' exemption.

div.head: MOORE FARMER'S SON BEFORE
div.p: MOORE FARMER'S SON BEFORE
APPEAL COURT.

At the Chester Appeal Tribunal, held at. Chester Castle on Tuesday, Mr. Arthur Browne (solicitor) applied, on behalf of Mr. Sandy Woodward, of the Village Farm, Moore, for the exemption of his son, Peter; who is his teamsman. The applicant's farm was 95 acres, 32 of which were sown with corn, and he had 21 milking cows, and sent 50 gallons- of milk per day into Warrington. After considering the matter, the Tribunal dismissed the appeal, on Captain Rigby, the military representative; undertaking not to call up the son to the colours until the Ist of October.

div.head: CHILDREN'S SUMMER CAMP.
div.p: CHILDREN'S SUMMER CAMP.
Mountains, Sea, Woods, And ..
Fine Weather.

Last Saturday the second group of 150 War- rington girls left the Gymnasium for the well- equipped summer Camp on the sand hills be- tween Prestatyn and lihyl. They were accom- panied by Miss Erason, Miss Spencer, Mr. Jenkins and Mr. Ransome. On arriving at their destination they were welcomed by the ladies who had given their services the previous week. Being placed in lines the children marched to the camp, where they, greatly enjoyed their first meal. As last week, the time has passed away pleasantly in playing games, paddling on the sea shore, and taking delightful walks. - -

On Tuesday the girls were taken over the mountains. The day was beautiful; from the sky overhead fell the hot rays of the sun, whose light seemed to colour the scene. The home- ward path lay through the woods, and the children arrived at camp footsore and weary, but nevertheless happy.

The week passed all too quickly, and Friday found 'them busy preparing their huts for the boys who will arrive to-day. The visitors are all in good health and seem to have derived great benefit from their short stay at the camp, saying good-bye to the mountains and sea with keen regret. The helpers, who have given their services, are:—Mrs. Roughsedge and Misses Maude Emson, Wainwright, Kilgallon, Pen- nington and Spencer; Miss Mary Emson, super- intendent.

div.p: Palace and hippodrome. A winner of many prizes in the swimming world, Miss Kathleen Gibson, who shares the title-role in "The Girl and the Seal," prefers snore to talk about her partner than herself.
The two seals she is touring with are not the innocents their conduct on the stage would

have us conclude. As a matter of fact, it was only last week that Qne of them gave Miss Gibson a black eye. It was not a point in an arranged boxing contest. "He was angry, very angry," said Miss Gibson.

"If anyone thinks it is an easy business training and looking after seals let him try it. They get angry on very little provocation, and in order to keep them under control I have to direct my eyes on them,all the time. It is a very risky act. They are not averse to biting lumps out of one. The trouble is that their bites are poisonous, and if they break the skin I have to neutralise the injury with a special substance.

"They won't do anything unless I keep giving them fish. Some people in the audience think I am throwing them biscuits, but they are scraps of fish. That is their only diet. Between them they have three barrels a week when they are working and two when they are not." Like certain politicians, they are very fond of herrings.

One seal is fifteen years old and senior by about five years to the other. They hail from California. The have been on the stage for most of their years and with this act for two or three. Working hard every day from eight o'clock in the morning until midnight (with intervals for refreshments) Miss Gibson was employed seven months making them stage perfect. Between them they give an interest- ing and sensational performance.

An excellent programme is announced for next week, that remarkable Hindoo magician, Linga-Singh, heading the bill. He does some wonderful things and is full of mystification. Also in the programme is Ed. E. Ford, from Australia. On another page will be seen—you cannot miss them—some amusing faoial ex- pressions. I think he can hold five or six golf balls in his spacious mouth at once. His is a most curious and interesting performance. Other turns announced include the Six Dandy Mascots and Orpheus (in an artistic musical interlude).

div.head: SOLDIERS' CONCERTS.
div.p: SOLDIERS' CONCERTS.
Double-Event! At The Raddon Court
Hospital.

In order to swell the fund of the Daresbury Division of the British Red Cross Society to- wards providing a motor ambulance to be pre- sented for use in Warrington and district, two concerts were held in the grounds of the Raddon Court Red Cross Hospital on Wednes- day. Ideal conditions prevailed, and there were good audiences at both concerts, which, com- menced at three o'clock and five o'clock respectively. The items were well sustained throughout and encores were numerous. The first pro- gramme was opened by a song, " March on to [Berlin," by Private Foster, who later on in the afternoon gave "Ragtime," and also took part in a quartet entitled "When you come home," I the other members of the party being Corporal Ward, Private Cairns and Private Scott. Gunner Elliott gave two comic songs, "No! No! No ! " and, "Far, far away." Corporal Ward, who possesses a fine rich voice, was heartily applauded for his renderings of "The long, long trail" and " The sunshine of your stnile." Private Vernon sang "Michael Cassidy," and Private Scott gave "The fox- trot." Miss Reynolds gave in a fine manner two violin solos, and Miss Trislove sang two songs. The same programme was delivered at the five o'clock performance. while several extra items were given. Mrs. Garnett recited very ably. and Private Botham sang two songs, "The deathless Army" and "Steen. sleep, sleep." Private Foster contributed "The Angelus." Tens were served during the day, and an rit- traetion was the appearance .amongst the audience of Mimi Yvonne, the little child actress.

div.head: MILITARY TRIBUNALS.
div.p: MILITARY TRIBUNALS.
BUSY BUSINESSES.
Indispensability Of Employes Urged By Employers.

A considerable number of business cases were dealt ;with by the Tribunal at the Town Hall on Tuesday. Mr. Swallow, solicitor, appeared for Mrs. Griffiths, licensee of the Cheshire Cheese, Latchford, who asked for exemption for her son, aged 38, a married man with two children, who has managed the business since her husband's death eight years ago. Mrs. Griffiths is 72 years of age and in poor health. Mr. Swallow pointed out that it was requisite owing to the situation of the house that it should be managed by a man. If applicant's. son was taken, she would only have to employ another man, and it would require someone having experience in the trade. The, Chairman (Dr. Joseph, deputy-mayor) said there.were other similar cases to this one, in which licensees' managers were concerned, which were adjourned until the Tribunal could consider the whole lot together, .taking into consideration, of course, the special points in individual cases. The present application would also be adjourned. • Mr. Swallow: To any particular date?
The Chairman: You will have notice of the decision.
Confectioner's Vanman.

Mr. C. H. Unsworth, solicitor, represented Messrs. Bennett and Son, bakers and confed- tioners, who applied for exemption for a van- man, aged 39.. There -was also an application by the man on domestic grounds, his wife being in delicate health. Applicant has five children. • In reply to the Tribunal, applicant said that he delivered goods in Warrington and Latch- ford. The firm had horse vans and motor vans, and some girls were employed. The employers' appeal was refused, and the decision on the man's domestic application was postponed pending more definite medical evi- dence as to the condition of the applicant's wife. Two Brothers Killed.

A moulder, married; with three children, applied for exemption. He mentioned that he was now earning about £2 a week. He had had two brothers killed in the war, and another is at present with the colours. He Stated that he had been employed .with a certain munitions firm, and had been stopped. He was the only married man stopped—a single man, 27, being kept in his place. • The Chairman (to the Military Representa- tive): Do you hear that, Capt. Mathams? Capt. Mathams : I do. The Chairman asked applicant how much he bad been earning with the munitions firm, and he replied from £3 to £4'a week. The Chairman: 'You ought to have a bank book with that.
The Applicant: I had one bank book for doctor's notes after finishing moulding. (Laugh- ter.) The appeal was refused. Metal Firm's Application.

Mr. Arthur Browne, solicitor, appeared 'for Messrs. G. Howard, a firm doing an extensive business in the metal trade, who sought exemp- tion for four of their employes and one of the partners. Mr. Browne detailed the large con- tracts which the firm had in hand at present, and the duties of the men referred to, who are all skilled wotkers. They were doing business with no fewer than 34 controlled firms in differ- ent parts of the country. The partner had to visit these places and superintend operations at the Folly-lane siding, where the premises were 34 acres in extent. The firm had at present two thousand tons of metal in scrap to be delivered, and the men were working on Saturdays and Sundays—seventy hours a week. All the firms they were supplying with metal were munition Manufacturers. Since the war eight men had gone to the Colours: There are eleven perma- nent men, all over military age except one, who had been six months in the Army and dis- charged sick. There were seven casual labourers.
The Tribunal granted conditional exemption in. the cases of all the men except one, in which the application was refused. The partner's case was adjourned. Demands of the Grocery Trade.

The extensive firm of Messrs. Henry Milling and Co., grocers and provision Merchants, War- rington, applied for exemption on behalf of three of their men. Mr. T. S. Steel explained that some employes had been called up, and that two other men were out sick. The application was in respect of men who were absolutely in- dispensable. Conditional exemption was granted in respect of two employes, while three months was allowed in the remaining case. An application by one of the directors of the firm, who has been passed for garrison duty, was again adjourned. Member of a firm making coffins and supply- ing funerals was given two months', final. He is an attested man, aged 38. When asked by Dr. Joseph if he had passed the (lector he replied. "Yes, sir, you passed me." Mr. T. S. Steel appeared for a travelling showman (houp-las, cocoanut shies, &c.), aged 34, married. He goes from town to town for weekly fairs, and rents frontages at so much per foot from local authorities. He said that in some cases these pitches were rented before- hand, being secured three months and even twelve months in advance.—Two months' exemption. Mr. Steel also represented a furniture dealer and mattress and bedding manufacturer, who asked for exemption for his principal employe, aged. 38 years. They manufactured something like 3,000 beds and mattresses during the year, and amongst other institutions, supplied mat- tresses to the WhitecroSs Hospital. This man also acted as clerk.—Two months' exemption.

div.head: "HAPPY TO GO."
div.p: "HAPPY TO GO."
Pianist Whose Wife Has Got A
Situation.

Another sitting was held at the Town 'Hall on Thursday morning. "My wife has now got a position in town, and in a few weeks I shall be most happy to go into the Army. I want to go," remarked a pianist, aged 39 sears. "But I should like t) see how she gets fon for a bit." The Tribunal gave him a month. Pawnbroker's Useful War Service.

Mr. Thomas Domville, a pawnbroker with three shops, said that at present he had four men, one of whom was over military age, and he appealed for the others, these being managers. Mr. Domville mentioned that since the war he had done about a thousand miles in his motor car on military work and 4,000 miles on Red Cross work. In his shops he was hard pressed, for, though his business was quieter in the pledge department, it was far busier than formerly in the sales department. Two of the men put in domestic appeals. These the .Tribunal dismissed, granting cOnditional exemption lon bu4iness grounds to one and giving a month's temporary exemption to the two others.

Mr. Domville said it would mean that he would have to close one of the shops. The Chairman (Councillor Joseph) advised him to try women, but Mr. Domville said he didn't like the idea of a lady managing a pawn- shop. The Chairman: It is astonishing what you can do if you are put to it. Mr. Dornville: I do not think I have been selfish. I have done my best. Thq Chairman: We cannot reverse our de- cision. We are very sorry. Later, the Chairman announced that fresh evidence had been brought forwar.l and, in4lbad of the exemptions being final, they would be allowed to remain open. Run On Mineral Waters.

Mr. Arthur Browne, solicitor, aPpeared for Messrs. Stothert and Sons, mineral water manu- facturers, who applied for a married man with five children. He looked after the machinery am' also drove one of the motor lorries during several hours of the day. In consequenc of the hot weather they were very busy, and the male employes had to work last Sunday to cope with the business. The firm paid a great deal of money under the new taxes. Before the :rar began they had eleven males, now they only had four. The man appealed for also put for- ward domestic grounds, these being that his wife was in ill-health as Well as several of his children.
Conditional exemption on both grounds.

div.head: FOREiGN, BUT NOT
div.p: FOREiGN, BUT NOT
TURKISH.
Shipping Clerk's Respite.

At the Warrington Rural District Tribunal on Wednesday the shipping clerk of a Man- chester firm engaged in the export cotton trade applied for conditional exemption on domestic grounds as well as on business grounds. His firm wrote stating that applicant was an ac- complished linguist and spoke Spanish and Portuguese. He was invaluable in their busi- ness and could not be replaced. Applicant had been previously granted three months' tem- porary exemption.......
The Rev. A. M. Mitchell: Is this an English fitm?

Applicant: A naturalised British film. The Chairman (Mr. George Mather): What country? • Applicant: Captain Mathams: It's not Turkish? Applicant: No. Temporary exemption was granted for two months—this decision to be final. Market Gardener. Mr. Arthur Browne appeared for a market gardener, of Croft, who applied for exemption in the case of his son, 22 years of age, unmar- ried. It was stated that applicant is unable through illness to attend to his business. Six acres of land are being cultivated as a market garden and are looked after by the son, who also attends to two greenhouses. There are also a horse and pony to take produce to Warring- ton Market, which the young man attends three times a week. Mr. Browne further ex- plained that applicant was in a pitiable con- dition with locomotor ataxy and unable to get up or downstairs. He had not seen the present crop sown in the land. Temporary exemption was granted until the end of September. Appeal Refused. An employe in a leather factory, whose work consists principally in stamping out boot soles, asked for further exemption; his firm having previously procured a concession for one month. He is 29 years of age, married, with one child, and had been passed for labour service at home or abroad. He stated that he contributed to the support of his father. He has four brothers, all married men, employed on muni- tions. The appeal was dismissed.

div.head: Brewer's Foreman.
div.p: Brewer's Foreman.

Mr. Richard Forshaw. Burtonwood Brewery, requested the Tribunal to grant exemption for the foreman in his bottling department, who is aged 36 and is a married man with six chil- dren. Seven girls were employed in the bottling department, and Mr. FOrshaw explained that quite a number of his employes had been taken.
Conditional exemption was agreed to. Other Cases.
The farm bailiff of the Padgate Cottage Homes, a married man, aged 37, and for whom his employers appealed, was .given three months' exemption.

div.head: MOORE FARMER'S SON BEFORE
div.p: MOORE FARMER'S SON BEFORE
APPEAL COURT.

At the Chester Appeal Tribunal, held at. Chester Castle on Tuesday, Mr. Arthur Browne (solicitor) applied, on behalf of Mr. Sandy Woodward, of the Village Farm, Moore, for the exemption of his son, Peter; who is his teamsman. The applicant's farm was 95 acres, 32 of which were sown with corn, and he had 21 milking cows, and sent 50 gallons of milk per day into Warrington. After considering the matter, the Tribunal dismissed the appeal, on Captain Rigby, the military representative; undertaking not to call up the son to the colours until the Ist of October.

div.head: CHILDREN'S SUMMER CAMP.
div.p: CHILDREN'S SUMMER CAMP.
Mountains, Sea, Woods, And
Fine Weather.

Last Saturday the second group of 150 War- rington girls left the Gymnasium for the well- equipped summer Camp on the sand hills be- tween Prestatyn and lihyl. They were accom- panied by Miss Emson, Miss Spencer, Mr. Jenkins and Mr. Ransotne. On arriving at theu. destination they were welcomed by the ladies who had given their services the previous week. Being placed in lines the children marched to the camp, where they greatly enjoyed their first meal. As last week, the time has passed away pleasantly in playing games, paddling on the sea shore, and taking delightful walks. . -

On Tuesday the girls were taken over •the mountains. The day was beautiful; from the sky overhead fell the hot rays of the sun, whose light seemed to colour the scene. The home- ward path lay through the woods, and the children arrived at camp footsore and weary, but nevertheless happy.

The week passed all too quickly, and Friday found 'them busy preparing their huts for the boys who will arrive to-day. The visitors are all in good health and seem to have derived great benefit from their short stay at the camp, saying good-bye to the mountains and sea with keen regret. The helpers, who have given their e services, are:—Mrs. Roughsedge an Misses Maude Emson, Wainwright, Kilgallon, Pen- nington and Spencer; Miss Mary Emson, super- intendent.

Palace and Hippodrome. A winner of many prizes in the swimming world, Miss Kathleen Gibson, who shares the title-role in "The Girl and the Seal," prefers 'more to talk about her partner than herself.

The two seals she is touring with are not the innocents their conduct on the stage would have us conclude. As a matter of fact, it was only last week that one of them gave Miss Gibson a black eye. It was not a point in an arranged boxing contest. "He was angry, very angry," said Miss Gibson.

"If anyone thinks it is an easy business training and looking after seals let him try it. They get angry on very little provocation, and in order to keep them under control I have to direct my eyes on them,all the time. It is a very risky act. They are not averse to biting lumps out of one. The trouble is that
their bites are poisonous, and if they break the skin I have to neutralise We injury with a special substance.

"They won't do anything unless I keep giving them fish. Some people in the audience think I am throwing them biscuits, but they are scraps of fish. That is their only diet. Between them they have three barrels a week when they are working and two when they are not." Like certain politicians, they are very fond of herrings.

One seal is fifteen years old and senior by about five years to the other. They hail from California. The have been on the stage for most of their years and with this act for two or three. Working hard every day from eight o'clock in the morning until midnight (with intervals for refreshments) Miss Gibson was employed seven months making them stage perfect. Between them they give an interest- ing and sensational performance.

An excellent programme is announced for next. week, that remarkable Hindoo magician, Linga-Singh, heading the bill. He does some wonderful things and is full of mystification. Also in the programme is Ed. E. Ford, from Australia. On another page will be seen—you cannot miss them—some amusing facial ex- pressions. I think he can hold five or six golf balls in his spacious mouth at once. His is a most curious and interesting performance. Other turns announced include the Six Dandy Mascots and Orpheus (in an artistic musical interlude).

div.p: SOLDIERS' CONCERTS.
Double-Eveni At The Raddon Court
Hospital.

In order to swell the fund of the Daresbury Division of the British Red Cross Society to- wards providing a motor ambulance to be pre- sented for use in Warrington and district, two concerts were held in' the grounds of the Raddon Court Red Cross Hospital on Wednes- day. Ideal conditions prevailed, and there were good audiences at both concerts, which, com- menced at three o'clock and five o'clock respectively. The items were well sustained throughout, and encores were numerous. The first pro- gramme was opened by a song, a March on to Berlin," by Private Foster, who later on in the afternoon gave "Ragtime," and also took part in a quartet entitled "When you come home," the other members of the party being .Corporal Ward, Private Cairns and Private Scott. Gunner Elliott gave two comic songs, "No! No! No! " and "Far, far away." Corporal Ward, who possesses a fine rich voice, was heartily applauded for his renderings of "The long, long trail" and a The sunshine of your smile." Private Vernon sang "Michael Cassidy," and Private Scott gave "The fox- trot." Miss Reynolds gave in a fine manner two violin solos, and Miss Trislove sang two songs. The same programme was delivered at the five o'clock performance. while several' extra items were given. Mrs. Garnett recited very ably, and Private Botham sang two songs, "The deathless Army" and "Sleep, sleep, sleep," Private Foster contributed "The Angelus." Tens were served during, the day, and an rit- traction was the appearance •amongst the audience of Mimi Yvonne, the little child actress.

RUGBY FOOTBALL. Friendly Matches To Be Played At Wilderspool. PATRIOTIC N.U. At. the annual meeting of the Northern Rugby Football Union, held in Huddersfield on Tues- day, it was unanimously decided to continue football next season on the same lines as last, the only alteration being the raising of the age limit for Intermediates from 18 to 20 years. The following amended resolutions were adopted : " That, excepting for schoolboys and Intermediate players under 20 years of age, all competitive football under Northern Union Rules, be suspended for the duration of the war." "That no club, union, body or official connected with the Northern Union shall be allowed to make any payment to players for broken time during the duration of the war." It will be remembered that the age limit was fixed at 18 last season so that there should be no interference with voluntary recruiting.. Now that all men of military age have to serve in one form or other there can be no objection to raising the age to 20 for available players. MOTOR AMBULANCE AS BIRTHDAY GIFT. After it had been decided to recommend the League, which has in hand in the Relief Fund the sum of £BO7 2s. 4d., to make grants to clubs in need of financial assistance, the Chair- man drew the attention of the representatives to the report, which stated that " on the 29th day of August' the union will have been in existence for a period of twenty-one years." "It is unfortunate," the report continued, "that the times are somewhat out of joint for the due celebration of such an event. . . • It is a source of gratification to the committae to feel that the players attached to the union have responded so nobly to the call to fight for their King and country, and it is fervently hoped that the casualties may be few and far between amongst those brave players who are risking their lives for their country's sake." Whilst it was worthy of some note, yet it was not considered, in the present circumstances, advisable to celebrate the pleasing event by any function of jollification, yet it was felt that it might be appropriate and popular to devote a portion of their funds to provide a motor ambulance and present it to the Gov- ernment. The sum of .1:3,000 had already been invested in War Loan, and there was a balance in the bank of nearly £l,OOO, out of which the ambulance, which would cost about £620, might be purchased. There would still remain a sum sufficient to tide them over present diffi- culties without touching the War Loan. The resolution was submitted and carried 'unanimously. Last year a grant of .t 250 was made to the Prince of Wales' Fund, so that the union may be congratulated upon its patriotism. RELIEF FOR NECESSITOUS CLUBS. A meeting of the Northern Rugby Football League was held at the close of the union meeting, when it was explained that at the beginning of last season it was felt that the Relief Fund should not be used for the purpose of playing friendly football, the League Man- agement Committee being of opinion that after the war there would be a big demand on the fund. A recommendation from the union meeting that the question of financing clubs that required assistance made it imperative that something- should he done, and it was decided that the relief fund should be used for the purpose of affording relief to necessi- tous clubs. ALL CLUBS TO PLAY. Under the changed conditions of military service all the clubs in membership will make an effort to play friendly football during the season, which opens next montk, _Warrington, 'Widnes and Wakefield Trinity falling in with. the others. A meeting of Lancashire secre- taries is to be held in Manchester on Tuesday evening, when fixtures will probably be ar- ranged and matters incidental to the game will he fully discussed. ,It is hoped that all those players who are engaged on munitions, or otherwise exempt from military service, will avail themselves of the opportunity afforded them of engaging in friendly combat. Matches will be arranged so as not to inter- fere with their work, and the recreation will be the means of keeping them physically fit for their labours.
